title: Shell profits double as oil prices rise due to Iran war
description: Shell's profits for the second quarter of the year have more than doubled after the Iran war pushed up oil prices.The oil giant posted profits of $9.8
body: Shell's profits for the second quarter of the year have more than doubled after the Iran war pushed up oil prices.The oil giant posted profits of $9.84bn (£7.37bn) for the April-to-June period, up from $4.26bn at the same point last year.The price of crude has risen since the outbreak of the US-Israel war with Iran due to major disruption to global supplies of oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG) through the Strait of Hormuz.But energy prices have also seen sharp swings during the conflict, which has boosted Shell's trading business.Shell chief executive Wael Sawan said the company's "operational performance enabled very strong results during another quarter of severe disruption in global energy markets".Together with its profits of $6.92bn for the first three months of the year it means Shell has seen a 70% surge in first-half earnings.Shell and other energy giants such as BP and Norway's Equinor have seen bumper profits this year, partly down to trading on oil price swings.Before the conflict began, the price of Brent crude, the global benchmark for oil prices, was around $73 a barrel.Since then, it has peaked above $120 but also fallen back below $100 as speculation has swirled over when the Strait of Hormuz will reopen.These big movements in the oil price can widen the gap between buying and selling prices which typically enables traders to make bigger profits.However, the conflict in the Middle East has also affected some of Shell's operations. Its LNG production in Qatar has been shut down since early March because of the conflict, and its Pearl gas-to-liquids facility in Qatar suffered "extensive damage" when it was hit by a missile attack in March. The company has said repairs could take about a year.Overall gas production fell to 631,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day for the April to June period, from 909,000 barrels per day in the first quarter, the firm said.Total oil and gas production in the first half of the year fell 16% compared with the first half of 2025, although Shell did point to new oil production in Brazil and the Gulf of America."The standout contribution came from Shell's trading operation, which once again demonstrated the value of its integrated business model, supported by healthy refining and chemicals performance and robust production growth in Brazil," said Maurizio Carulli, global energy analyst at Quilter Cheviot."[Shell] remains a steady ship in an industry where conditions can change rapidly."However, environmental campaigners reacted with anger to the latest results."With extreme heatwaves and wildfires hitting the UK and ravaging Europe, it's outrageous that Shell is making huge profits while continuing to fuel the climate crisis," said Friends of the Earth energy campaigner Danny Gross."These profits have been built on an energy crisis that's left households across the country struggling with high energy bills at home and expensive fuel at the pumps. This underlines the urgent need to end our dependence on costly oil and gas."

schema.headline: Shell profits double as oil prices rise due to Iran war

title: Greek police probe 'foul play' in death of woman found in suitcase
description: Image source, FacebookImage caption, A photo of Elisabeth-Jane Ross which appeared to have been taken in 2015ByMary McCoolBBC ScotlandGreek police hav
body: Image source, FacebookImage caption, A photo of Elisabeth-Jane Ross which appeared to have been taken in 2015ByMary McCoolBBC ScotlandGreek police have said they are trying to determine whether foul play was involved in the death of a Scottish woman whose body was found in a suitcase.Elisabeth-Jane Ross, 38, was found in an abandoned building in the Kypseli district of Athens on 18 July, reportedly by a homeless man.She is believed to have died between five and seven days before she was found and is thought to have travelled to Greece from Cyprus two weeks before her death.A spokesperson for police in Greece told the BBC: "We are awaiting the results of the toxicology tests to determine the cause of death and ascertain whether foul play was involved, as this was not clarified by the initial examination of the body."Image source, EUROKINISSIImage caption, Greek police at the scene in the Kypseli district in AthensFirst Minister John Swinney said Ross's family would be supported by the Scottish government and the Foreign and Commonwealth Office.He said: "This is an absolutely appalling case that has been reported overnight."And obviously I'm deeply concerned that such a tragedy has taken place."Helena Smith, The Guardian's correspondent in Athens, told BBC Radio Scotland that the body was found in a derelict building in downtown Athens, "in an area that is booming, full of Airbnbs".She said: "It is very popular with people travelling through Athens and young foreigners who have elected to make the Greek capital their home."Smith said that Ross had family in Edinburgh and "connections" to Greece - staying with a friend in Athens before she disappeared.She added: "It would seem that someone had control over her mobile phone after she died and was sending messages to distract the authorities and close friends from trying to track her down."On Wednesday the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) confirmed they were providing consular support and were in contact with the Greek authorities.A Police Scotland spokesperson said: "We are aware of the death of Scottish woman in Athens and are liaising with authorities in Greece."Officers are providing support to her family in Scotland."Interpol said it was not able to comment on individual cases.

schema.headline: Greek police probe 'foul play' in death of woman found in suitcase

title: Missile that left crater deep inside Poland was probably Russian - Polish PM Tusk
description: Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk has said an object that crashed into a field in eastern Poland in the early hours of Thursday was probably a Russian
body: Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk has said an object that crashed into a field in eastern Poland in the early hours of Thursday was probably a Russian missile.The unidentified object caused a 10m-wide (33ft) crater a short distance from the village of Tarnawa Kolonia, 92km (57 miles) from the border with Ukraine during a large-scale Russian attack on the cities of Lviv, Kyiv and near Kryvyhi Rih.Tusk said initially that "all the indications" were that the missile that violated Polish airspace was a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile, during a specially convened meeting in the eastern city of Lublin.He then went to the site of the incident and said that according to military experts the majority of "recovered fragments point to it being a Russian Kh-101 missile".Although no casualties had been reported in Thursday's incident near Tarnawa Kolonia, the Polish prime minister made clear it was being taken very seriously. There was no immediate threat as it had not landed in a built-up area, he said, adding that "we were prepared to shoot it down if had continued its flight".Nato said it was in close contact with Polish authorities and the Supreme Allied Commander in Europe, Gen Alexus G Grynkewich, said the Western defensive alliance would "continue to take all necessary measures to defend Nato territory".Polish Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said about 20 objects were seen close to Polish airspace overnight and pyrotechnical analysis was being carried out.Ukraine's acting Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha had earlier declared definitively that a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile had "crossed into Poland as part of Russia's massive strike against Ukraine, violating Nato airspace".Tusk said he was in contact with fellow European leaders and the head of the European Council António Costa said Russia's "massive combined strike against Ukraine" had underlined again that "Russia's aggression is a threat to the security as a whole". At least eight people died and dozens more were wounded across Ukraine, including six members of one family in a village near Kryvyih Rih. Dozens more were wounded in Lviv, not far from Ukraine's western border with Poland.A number of Russian drones and one unarmed Russian missile have landed in Poland since Russia's full-scale war in Ukraine began in February 2022. Two Polish farmers were killed by a missile that landed just over the border from Ukraine in November 2022, but that was believed to have been a Ukrainian air defence missile responding to a Russian attack.Poland's military detected the object at about 03:40 on Thursday (01:40 GMT) and sent an F-16 fighter jet to intercept it before it disappeared minutes later from radar systems. A military helicopter was then sent to search the area.Air raid sirens blared in Lublin and Krasnystaw further to the south-east because of the Russian airstrikes in neighbouring Ukraine. Residents in Tarnawa Kolonia reported hearing a loud bang at about 04:00 and police found the crash site about an hour later.The Polish leader had met Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in Lublin the previous evening as Zelensky was returning from talks with US President Donald Trump.

schema.headline: Missile that left crater deep inside Poland was probably Russian - Polish PM Tusk

title: Prison recalls up 28% in England and Wales, new figures reveal
description: Large rise in offenders sent back to prison, figures revealByTom Edgington and Harriet AgerholmBBC VerifyThere has been a large rise in the number of
body: Large rise in offenders sent back to prison, figures revealByTom Edgington and Harriet AgerholmBBC VerifyThere has been a large rise in the number of offenders being recalled to prisons in England and Wales having been released on licence, new government figures show.There were 51,419 licence recalls in the year ending March 2026, up from 40,259 in the previous year - a 28% increase.Although recalls in January to March were slightly lower than the previous three-month period, they remain well above historical levels.The figures follow government schemes to release a number of offenders early in an effort to ease prison overcrowding.The Ministry of Justice (MOJ) said offenders released on licence face strict conditions "and can be hauled back to prison if they break these rules".Cassia Rowland, from the Institute for Government think tank, said most recalls are for breaches of licence conditions, such as missed appointments, rather than offenders committing further offences or posing a serious risk to the public."The probation service is overwhelmed, with high caseloads and lots of vacancies putting often inexperienced staff under huge pressure," she said.The most common reason provided for prison recalls between January and March was "non-compliance" (9,683), followed by "failed to keep in touch" (5,025).There were 2,891 recalls because an offender faced further charges between January and March 2026, a 23% rise on the same period in 2025. More than one reason can be recorded against each recall.Alex Hewson, from the Prison Reform Trust, said: "Many leave prison facing challenges such as addiction, poor mental health and unstable housing, making compliance with licence conditions difficult."Responding to the figures, the MOJ said "public protection is our priority" and the statistics "show that we do not hesitate to recall offenders to prison when the risk escalates."Sentencing Act release scheme pausedThe increase in prisoner recall comes after the government introduced an early release scheme in England and Wales to help ease overcrowding pressure in September 2024.The scheme meant eligible prisoners could be released after serving 40% of their sentence rather than half.As of March 2026, 70,066 people had been released under the scheme, external.Rowland says early release schemes have contributed to the increase in recalls."But these schemes have also made it harder for prisons and probation to prepare people for release effectively and give them support with basic things like finding accommodation, accessing job support and so on."Despite the releases there were still 86,267 people in England and Wales' prisons, external as of 27 July, meaning the prison estate was 97% full.In a further attempt to ease prison capacity pressure, Sir Keir Starmer's government had planned to release some offenders after serving just one-third of their custodial term.The Sentencing Act release scheme was due to come into force from 2 September, but it has been paused by new Prime Minister Andy Burnham following criticism from survivors and victims' families.The BBC understands around 700 prisoners would have been eligible for early release under the scheme's first phase.Although the prison population has remained relatively stable since 2010, following rapid growth in the 1990s, government projections, external suggest it could rise to about 90,000 in 2028.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Andy Burnham has announced a pause to the Sentencing Act early release schemeUsing early release to manage prison overcrowding is not new.Governments led by Labour and the Conservatives have each introduced emergency measures when the prison system has come under strain.In October 2023, Rishi Sunak's Conservative government began releasing eligible offenders up to 18 days early. The scheme was eventually expanded to up to 70 days ahead of offenders' release date.Nick Hardwick, the former chief inspector of prisons, says early release alone will not solve the problem, arguing "it's just going to slow the rate of growth".New prison plansThe Starmer government announced a plan to add 14,000 new prison places by 2031, external, including four new prisons. It said it would acquire land if necessary and would "make sure the supply always keeps up with demand".The MOJ previously told BBC Verify the government had delivered about 3,200 prison places so far - 1,600 for each of their two years in office. However, this figure only covers new prison places and does not factor in those taken out of use.Hardwick says expanding the number of prisons is only part of the answer because "the one thing you can't do quickly is produce experienced staff."The prison building programme is already costing billions of pounds, he adds, leaving it up to ministers to decide how much they are prepared to spend to keep more people in prison for longer."There's no perfect solution... it's a question of what's the least bad option."Additional reporting by Isobel Cottam

schema.headline: Prison recalls up 28% in England and Wales, new figures reveal

title: England on track for record heat-related deaths this year, UKHSA estimates
description: England is on track this year for the highest number of heat-related deaths since records began, according to estimates by the UK Health Security Agen
body: England is on track this year for the highest number of heat-related deaths since records began, according to estimates by the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA).In a preliminary assessment, it said there were an estimated 2,877 heat-related deaths during the May and June heatwaves, almost double the figure for the whole of last year.An estimated 753 deaths were associated with the 24-27 May heatwave and a further 2,124 with the one from 21-28 June. Definitive figures are expected in early 2027.Both spells broke Met Office UK monthly temperature records, with 35.1C (95.2F) recorded at Kew Gardens on 26 May and 38.0C recorded at Lingwood, Norfolk on 26 June.The current record for heat-related deaths was set in 2022, when 2,985 deaths were recorded.Report author Dr Ross Thompson, from the UKHSA, said "while the figures are interim, they suggest that, if we experience more periods of hot weather this summer, we could see the highest number of heat-associated deaths on record".Thompson added: "These figures highlight the significant danger that very hot weather can pose to people's health."This is particularly true for those who are more vulnerable including older adults and people with underlying medical conditions."He said "as the climate becomes warmer, we can expect periods of hot weather to become longer, more frequent and more extreme", adding that it is vital the country is prepared to deal with higher temperatures.Earlier this week parts of the UK sweltered through another heatwave that peaked on Wednesday, with temperature reaching 35.2C in Writtle, Essex.Cooler conditions and some rain are on the way for some on Thursday and into the weekend, but likely not in the driest areas.On Wednesday drought was declared across more than half of England due to hot, dry weather taking its toll on the country's water supplies.The Environment Agency (EA) said the drought covers much of central, eastern and southern England, with director of water Helen Wakeham saying the weather "means we are currently using water faster than nature can replenish it". Health Secretary Yvette Cooper said the sweltering heat has had a "serious impact this summer on people's health and on our NHS". She added: "My thoughts are with all those who have lost loved ones as a result of the long and intense heatwaves in recent months. "And my heartfelt thanks go to the NHS staff, care workers and emergency responders who have worked tirelessly through these exceptionally busy and challenging months to protect and care for people affected by the heat."May's heatwave smashed the temperature record for that month, with a high of 35.1C recorded at Kew Gardens. It surpassed the previous high of 32.8C set back in 1922 and equalled in 1944.A month later, June's heatwave set another monthly temperature record - 38.0C in Lingwood, Norfolk. The previous high was 35.6C set in 1957 and equalled during the infamous 1976 heatwave.Both were caused by a "heat dome" - a stalled area of high pressure that trapped hot air over the region.It is not just the UK that has dealt with sweltering temperatures this summer, as much of western Europe has also faced record-breaking temperatures.In the last week deadly wildfires have hit parts of France, Spain and Greece - with tens of thousands of people forced to evacuate their homes.

schema.headline: England on track for record heat-related deaths this year, UKHSA estimates

title: Arran Strong: Tributes paid as search called off for British surfer lost at sea
description: Tributes have been paid to surfer Arran Strong, after searches for the Briton who went missing off the coast of Portugal were called off.The Autoridad
body: Tributes have been paid to surfer Arran Strong, after searches for the Briton who went missing off the coast of Portugal were called off.The Autoridade Maritima Nacional (AMN) confirmed to BBC Sport that its search for the 28-year-old, which started soon after he went missing on Monday morning, was halted on Thursday.Strong, who lived in Portugal, had competed in the World Surf League for 10 years and represented Great Britain at each of the previous two World Surfing Games - finishing as the highest ranked British representative on both occasions."Beyond his performances in the water, Arran was a fantastic team-mate, respected competitor and a kind, generous presence whose passion for surfing left a lasting impression on everyone who had the privilege of knowing him," GB Surfing said in a statement on Instagram, external on Tuesday."His passing is a devastating loss to our sport and the wider surfing community, and he will be greatly missed."Our thoughts and heartfelt condolences are with Arran's family, friends, team-mates and all those whose lives he touched."The AMN said it was alerted to Strong getting into difficulties in the water off the Atlantic coast in southern Portugal at 11.33 BST on Monday.It said: "The young man disappeared at sea while crossing from Monte Clerigo beach to Carrapateira."His friend, who was with him, was rescued by a local fishing boat that was nearby."The friend was Strong's coach, Jose Maria Pyrrait, who said he did not see the moment in which Strong went missing.Pyrrait wrote on Instagram, external that they had stopped to drink water and take photos, before setting off again with Strong initially in the lead, before the coach overtook him."When I stopped to wait, I saw your board drifting about 100 meters away," he wrote. "I paddled as fast as I could to get there, diving repeatedly looking for you, but we were in a deep area and visibility was very short. I called my partner on land for help, who automatically activated the rescue."Pyrrait said they had spent another two and a half hours looking for Strong from the boat."Arran was like a son to me. From the age of 10 he trained with me and spent weekends and holidays with me, as his mother said, he was like a son of divorced parents. My love for him, was like another son that life gave me," he wrote."Rest in peace my 'son'."Tributes were paid from many of Strong's team-mates and friends in surfing.GB Surfing performance coach Luke Dillon wrote: "Hearts so heavy. Fought so many battles and lived life to the fullest always carrying a smile and infectious laugh. Sending love to Arran's family and friends."Eight-time British national champion Lucy Campbell wrote: "The world is going to miss that smile so much. Sending my love and hugs to you all."Fellow English women's surfing champion Alys Barton wrote: "Arran, we competed together for so many years and you were always the one encouraging everyone around you."Thank you for always smiling, believing in others and lifting everyone up. You will be deeply missed."

schema.headline: Arran Strong: Tributes paid as search called off for British surfer lost at sea

title: Fossil hunter discovers rare 'sea dragon' at Lavernock Point
description: Mountaineer who began fossil hunting after near-death experience discovers rare 'sea dragon'Image source, Ceri OakesImage caption, Fossil hunter Matth
body: Mountaineer who began fossil hunting after near-death experience discovers rare 'sea dragon'Image source, Ceri OakesImage caption, Fossil hunter Matthew Myerscough says finding fossils like this ichthyosaur in Somerset has helped him to recover after a near-death accidentByPaul PigottBBC WalesA mountaineer who nearly died in an avalanche has described how his recovery led him to amateur fossil hunting and the discovery of a marine reptile or "sea dragon" not found in Wales before.Matthew Myerscough said he was left with post-traumatic stress disorder after being unconscious for 20 minutes buried beneath a metre of snow after a slide on Yr Wyddfa, also known as Snowdon, in 2014.It led him away from the mountains to fossil-laden beaches at Lavernock Point in the Vale of Glamorgan, where he discovered a jaw bone from the Jurassic period 200 million years ago.Myerscough, a civil engineer, said the painstaking process of fossil hunting helped his worries and stresses to "melt away"."Looking back now, I realise, I have had some PTSD, external," he said of the accident. Myerscough returned to Yr Wyddfa in 2018 for the Dragon's Back Challenge, hiking past the place where he had almost died, but said by then he was moving away from mountaineering. "Being on the beach, and looking for fossils, and being kind of really focused on one specific task... it has been a tool for me to kind of process things," he said.  "Worries or stresses kind of melt away as you're focused," he said, comparing it to the mindfulness people can get from yoga, sport or watching a film.Image source, Matthew MyerscoughImage caption, Matthew Myerscough says fossil hunting is a wonderful activityAs well as helping his mental health, fossil hunting also led Myerscough to the discovery of a 201m-year-old plesiosaur jawbone, a type of marine reptile from the early Jurassic period which had never been found in Wales before. He and two fellow fossil hunters were walking away from Lavernock Point when they spotted a large shape in the limestone. Myerscough said that through contacting experts, they were able to establish that it was the lower jaw of a rhomaleosaurus, a carnivore also known as a sea dragon. Research on the find by National Museum Cardiff continues and Myerscough said he hoped it would lead to the publication of an academic paper. "Every now and again, whether it's a five-year-old or a 50-year-old, somebody finds something that is scientifically important, new to science, and we learn from that." What is fossil hunting?Myerscough said fossil hunting was all about looking for patterns in the rocks."I'm very much focused on using my eyes to find the fossils, so there's definitely plenty of trips where I'll go out and my hammer will stay in my rucksack."He said he carries a hand lens for taking a closer look at a rock that catches his eye, as well good hiking boots or wellies, and a flask of strong coffee."If you head towards Lavernock Point you can literally walk along the beach, and you may pick up a vertebra loose in the shingle from a plesiosaur or an ichthyosaur. "You can find bits of ribs, you can find coprolites, the fossilized poo from these animals and from prehistoric sharks."You can find all those fossils just loose, you know, in the shingle there, if you're lucky, and many families do, and I think that's such a wonderful pastime."Image source, Matthew MyerscoughImage caption, Limestone shale cliffs line the coast in the Vale of GlamorganMyerscough said much writing about archaeology focused on the discipline itself, but he has written a book - In Search of Sea Dragons: A Fossil Hunter's Odyssey - on the process of fossil hunting. "I wanted to read about the experience of actually finding fossils, you know, what it was like to actually discover something on the beach," he said. He suggested that fossil hunters can sometimes be secretive about their process, especially the location of their finds. "I'd seen photos of specimens, but perhaps the details of just where exactly they came from, or what they looked like when they were found was kind of shrouded in secrecy."I wanted to put this out there and say, 'This is what I found, this is what it was like when I found it, this is how I collected and recovered it, and this is what it meant to me," he said.

schema.headline: Fossil hunter discovers rare 'sea dragon' at Lavernock Point

title: Beauty Pie: Founder Marcia Kilgore on how she built five businesses
description: Beauty Pie founder on how she dropped out of university and built five beauty businessesFigure caption, Essential business tips from the Beauty Pie bo
body: Beauty Pie founder on how she dropped out of university and built five beauty businessesFigure caption, Essential business tips from the Beauty Pie bossByYasmin RufoBusiness reporter Updated 00:02 BSTThe name Marcia Kilgore might not be instantly recognisable but her Beauty Pie brand is known the world over for being an industry game-changer with its online-only subscription model.Before founding Beauty Pie in 2016, Kilgore had built other brands including luxury day spa Bliss, make-up and skincare range Soap & Glory and footwear brand FitFlop.Here the 57-year-old serial entrepreneur shares her story and the five secrets to success she learned along the way.1. You don't need a perfect planKilgore didn't always know she wanted to be an entrepreneur but growing up she saw first-hand the stress that financial insecurity could cause."I remember deciding at eight-years-old that when I was my parents' age, I would never want to be stressed about my electric bill," she says. That desire shaped her approach to work and risk. "I knew that working for other people wouldn't necessarily give me the freedom I wanted and at least when you are an entrepreneur, the risk is your own."She didn't begin with a grand business plan - she moved from Canada to New York to study at Columbia University and her tuition plan fell through so she had to get a job to support herself."You can't sit around thinking: 'What am I going to do? You have to survive. I knew I had to use the skills I had to support myself and then I would figure it out."She started working as a personal trainer and taking beauty classes in the evening."What ended up transpiring was that I was quite good at the beauty industry job," she says and eventually she dropped out of university to pursue a career in it.2. Know the job inside outImage source, Marcia KilgoreImage caption, Kilgore sold a majority stake of Bliss to LVMH in 1999Working in her salon, Kilgore says she was involved in every aspect of the business from the laundry, to performing treatments and training staff. She says that practical experience was invaluable when she later opened Bliss Spa in London in the 1990s. "I had trained loads of people ahead of the store opening but when we first opened it was so busy and a lot of them got afraid and quit."The good thing is I know how to wax and do facials so I could do all of the appointments myself." Her advice is to start a business in an area where you have genuine knowledge."You want to have deep expertise, so you're not left swinging in the wind if people disappoint you or things come in from the side and surprise you," she says.3. Challenge your own ideasImage source, Marcia KilgoreImage caption, Marcia Kilgore has founded brands including FitFlop, Soap and Glory and Beauty PieKilgore recommends asking yourself why someone should care about your idea and be able to explain the value of an idea in one clear sentence. "If you can't answer 'so what?' in one sentence, your idea isn't good enough yet."That doesn't necessarily mean abandoning it but it needs to be refined more so its purpose is immediately understandable, she says.Kilgore also warns against developing "ownership bias", believing an idea is brilliant simply because it belongs to them."You might think something is really great, but you're living in your own bubble," she says.Her advice is to "test your idea with your target market before you go too far down the road of investing in something nobody cares about but you". She adds that AI now offers significant opportunities to people starting their own business as "you don't need a huge budget for consultants". "AI can spit your idea back and forth, challenge it and advise you on what you need to consider that you might not obviously see."4. Expect sacrifice and be kindWhen she was starting out in her career Kilgore realised she needed to be "someone that people look forward to being around".It's important to be polite, punctual and nice as those qualities help you build loyalty, she says."I made sure I was the sunniest, hardest working and most diligent person to do that service.""If you do a really great job, people will recommend you," she says and she soon opened a tiny beauty salon that became booked up months in advance.She also explains you also need to be "willing to make some big sacrifices" to make your business successful."You're not going to have a lot of free time," she says as running a business requires you to be aware of changing customer behaviour, new competitors and wider market trends.That often means reading, researching and connecting ideas outside of working hours.Kilgore says the workload can feel easier if you have a curiosity around you as "that's what drives you". She does have some non-negotiables and has made an effort not to miss important events while raising her children, including school plays and family holidays.5. Do the deathbed testA test that Kilgore has used throughout her career is the deathbed test where she asks whether a project will still feel worthwhile at the end of her life."Imagine you're on your deathbed, think about what you would have done differently and do that," she says."If it doesn't mean something, or you haven't done something good for people, are you going to feel that your life was really well spent?"She adds that success for her isn't just about building another company but deciding which ideas are worth the time it will take to build them.

schema.headline: Beauty Pie: Founder Marcia Kilgore on how she built five businesses

title: US launches 'heavy' strikes on Iran after attempted attack on American troops
description: The US military says it has completed a "heavy wave" of strikes against Iran in retaliation for Tuesday's attempted ballistic missile attacks on Ameri
body: The US military says it has completed a "heavy wave" of strikes against Iran in retaliation for Tuesday's attempted ballistic missile attacks on American forces.Centcom said it hit "dozens" of Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) targets in response to Iran's firing on US bases in Jordan and at ships in the Strait of Hormuz.Iranian state media said the latest strikes had killed three people, including a two-year-old child, on Qeshm island, while other locations were also hit in the south and west of the country.The latest hostilities come on a week that has seen the conflict expand, with the first publicly announced joint US-Saudi strikes targeting Iranian proxies in Iraq.Iran and the US have engaged in escalating strikes and counter-strikes since a ceasefire in April, aimed at pausing the months-long war, fell apart in June. The US has blockaded Iranian ports and bombed Iranian sites, while Iran has fired missiles and drones at US assets in countries across the Middle East and targeted shipping in the economically important Strait of Hormuz, connecting the Gulf and Arabian Sea.On Wednesday, news outlet Axios cited an unnamed US official as saying that Trump had met Saudi defence minister Prince Khalid bin Salman, who had conveyed that Saudi Arabia wants to de-escalate tensions. The BBC has contacted the White House for comment. Analysis: Saudi Arabia's dilemma as it tries to stay out of US-Iran warMeanwhile, the Egyptian government said a fire at a port on Wednesday had been caused by a drone attack. Egypt, a US ally, has not previously been directly attacked during the war.The US-Iran conflict has reignited after several days of relative calm.For days, both sides halted strikes as talks apparently restarted in hopes of some type of diplomatic solution. Trump called them "very friendly negotiations", though Tehran denied any discussions were happening. But following the Iranian missile attack on a US base in Jordan on Tuesday, Trump vowed to retaliate, telling reporters at the White House: "We're going to be hitting them very hard because it's our turn to hit them.  They know it's coming. They asked us not to do it."The latest wave of US strikes started at 20:00 ET on Wednesday (01:00 BST on Thursday) and lasted about an hour, with Centcom calling them a "powerful response to yesterday's attempted Iranian attacks on US forces based in the Middle East". All of Iran's missiles were intercepted, Centcom said. The attack by the US targeted "military command centers, missile and drone facilities, coastal surveillance and defense sites, and maritime capabilities," Centcom wrote once the strikes were complete.Iranian state media agency Irib reported that the islands of Qeshm and Abadan, both central to the oil industry, were among the areas hit.  "A US attack on a residential home in the Chah Tangu neighbourhood of Qeshm killed three members of a family: the father, the mother, and their 2-year-old child," Fars reported citing the Hormozgan University of Medical Sciences.A man in his 30s living in the south of the island told BBC Persian he was heading to Tehran, because "things are becoming more dangerous here"."Our internet situation has been a mess. The electricity has been cutting out several times since this morning," he said. "There have been loud bangs since 03:40 this morning. We are helpless."Meanwhile, Jordan's armed forces said that air defence systems had successfully shot down five Iranian missiles targeting the Kingdom's territory on Thursday.On Tuesday, the IRGC said it had targeted a US air base and a command centre in Jordan "in response to the acts of aggression of the American child-killing army".It also said naval forces had struck three oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz after they "ignored warnings" and sailed along what it described as an "unsafe and illegal route" through the vital Gulf waterway.Last Friday, Trump suspended an intensive bombing campaign that had lasted for 13 consecutive nights. The US said it had targeted Iranian weapons and military sites. Scores of people were reported to have died.On Tuesday, Centcom said the joint US-Saudi strikes hit "multiple terrorist logistics and weapons sites across eastern Iraq in a strong response to over 30 IRGC-directed aerial drone attacks in the last 72 hours".Iraq's paramilitary Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF), which is dominated by Iran-backed Shia militias, said at least 20 of its members had been killed in US-Saudi strikes on its bases.The Iraqi presidency said it denounced the bombing of the PMF bases, calling it "an unacceptable attack and a blatant violation of Iraq's sovereignty".But Trump told Fox News the strikes had been "co-ordinated with the Iraqi government".Saudi Arabia, which sees itself as the leading Sunni Muslim power, and Iran, the largest Shia Muslim country, have been locked in a struggle for regional dominance for decades.With additional reporting from Ghoncheh Habibiazad, BBC Persian

schema.headline: US launches 'heavy' strikes on Iran after attempted attack on American troops

title: Djed Spence: Tottenham boss Roberto de Zerbi tells England defender to stay at club
description: Tottenham manager Roberto de Zerbi says he wants to convince England defender Djed Spence to stay at the club amid uncertainty over his future.The 25-
body: Tottenham manager Roberto de Zerbi says he wants to convince England defender Djed Spence to stay at the club amid uncertainty over his future.The 25-year-old, who signed a long-term deal with the club last year, has been linked with a move to Inter Milan and Everton.De Zerbi says he sees Spence as an important part of his plans despite increased competition in his role after a summer of significant spending.Spurs have spent a club record £237m so far this summer as they rebuild their squad after narrowly avoiding relegation on the final day of last season's Premier League."I repeat what I said to Djed, and to Lucas [Bergvall]," De Zerbi said, referencing comments he made about the in-demand Sweden midfielder a day earlier."I would like you to stay if you want to stay. If you don't want to stay, if you want to leave, then you have to leave."Spence started in 23 of his 30 Premier League appearances last year as Spurs finished 17th for the second season in a row.Spain's World Cup winner Pedro Porro currently occupies Spence's preferred right-back position at Tottenham.De Zerbi said he regarded Porro as the "best in the world" in his role.Captain Cristian Romero is among those likely to leave the club.Romero was criticised for his decision to fly back to Argentina while injured before the final game of the season - a match for which he did ultimately return.De Zerbi said it was wrong to criticise Romero for his initial decision, saying he had shown "unbelievable behaviour" during the Italian's time at the club, but accepted it was "his will" to leave."At the beginning of my time in April I had, I don't know, one million individual meetings. And the players told me if they are (staying) here (or not)," he said."I said: 'Yes, help me to stay up, and then I help you to leave. If you don't help me to stay up, you stay underwater with me.'"Italian goalkeeper Guglielmo Vicario is also expected to depart after losing his place to Antonin Kinsky.Earlier this month, Spurs broke their transfer record twice in two days, first signing midfielder Mateus Fernandes from West Ham for £85m before bringing in Sandro Tonali from Newcastle for £100m.Jan Paul van Hecke has also joined from Brighton in a £52m deal, alongside the free transfers of experienced trio Marcos Senesi, Andrew Robertson and Martin Dubravka.De Zerbi says his side are targeting another attacking signing alongside their pursuit of Manchester City's Savinho.The Brazilian is among the attacking players in advanced talks over a move to north London, with Spurs also pursuing another unnamed target.Speaking in Sydney, De Zerbi said: "The transfer market is not finished for sure, but we have completed 60% of our project. Now we have another 'bomba'."Asked whether he was referring to a winger or a striker, the former Brighton and Marseille manager replied: "Attackers."I don't love working with plan A, plan B, plan C. It is plan A, full stop, because all players are not the same. "We have to increase the number of goals."De Zerbi said he had been like a "shark" this summer while pursuing targets.

schema.headline: Djed Spence: Tottenham boss Roberto de Zerbi tells England defender to stay at club

title: Virtual interviews don't show bosses your personality, says Burnham
description: Speaking to former political adviser Jimmy McLoughlin on his podcast Jimmy's Jobs of the Future, Burnham said he was concerned that the use of technol
body: Speaking to former political adviser Jimmy McLoughlin on his podcast Jimmy's Jobs of the Future, Burnham said he was concerned that the use of technology was not making recruitment processes "fairer"."How do you get over some of your personality, your passion?" he asked, referring to virtual interviews. "It seems to me to then work against people who have that side to their character and work for those who are just giving the more formulaic answer."I do worry about that and I've seen that in relation to my kids and their situation."Responding to Burham's comments, industry body the Recruitment and Employment Confederation (REC) said online interviews were useful, particularly in earlier hiring stages, but could not replace vital in-person connection. Maxine Bligh, chief membership and innovation officer at the REC, added: "AI tools are helpful, even essential, when dealing with a huge volume of applications, but it takes skill and professionalism to make the right call."The key message from us to recruiters is to go digital where it matters and human where it counts."Elizabeth Anderson, chief executive of the Digital Poverty Alliance, said online interviews allowed people who don't live in cities to access opportunities."Forcing young people to travel into London and other major cities or be limited to local roles that are often in short supply, doesn't support aspiration or opportunity within the UK," she said."AI is the bigger issue. AI in job interviews and CV sorting is unfair on young people due to its inherent bias and the vast majority of school leavers being unaware of how to write to be shortlisted by the AI recruitment tools doing the sorting."More than one million 16-25-year-olds are not in education, employment or training - the highest level in more than 12 years, official figures show.A major review by former minister Alan Milburn found job and career opportunities for young people are "not growing, they're shrinking" with one in six set to be out of work, education or training in five years unless action is taken."We are at risk of a lost generation" with young adults facing a "perfect storm" of challenges, Milburn warned in May.

schema.headline: Virtual interviews don't show bosses your personality, says Burnham

title: Thousands evacuated in Crete as Europe battles wildfires
description: Thousands of people have been evacuated on the Greek island of Crete as wildfires fanned by strong winds menace tourist resorts and villages.Two firef
body: Thousands of people have been evacuated on the Greek island of Crete as wildfires fanned by strong winds menace tourist resorts and villages.Two firefighters died on the island on Wednesday when they became trapped while tackling a fire near Krya Vrysi in the Rethymno region. A third firefighter died on the Greek mainland, near the port town of Gytheio in the Peloponnese. As gusts reached 125km/h (77mph) on the island, around 8,000 people were evacuated from their homes overnight but were later allowed to return.Greece is among many European countries facing devastating fires and drought. Several fires have continued to burn in Spain and Portugal, although Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez declared an end to the national emergency for wildfires in the Ávila and Madrid regions.In south-west France some residents have been able to return to their homes after a major wildfire in the Gironde region.The fire raging in Crete broke out in the Rethymno region on Wednesday and has since spread rapidly, destroying homes and agricultural land. It remains one of the biggest fires currently active on the island and is still burning out of control.Meanwhile, wildfires have erupted in the north-western Spanish provinces of Zamora and León, not far from the border with Portugal, with more than 1,000 people evacuated.Five people were injured in a fire in the eastern town of Valpaços in Portugal, according to local reports.A major fire that consumed an area in excess of 66,000 hectares to the west of the Spanish capital, Madrid, and caused tens of thousands of people to be evacuated has stopped spreading, allowing some residents to return home.As he ended the national emergency in the area, Pedro Sánchez urged "extreme caution" during the fourth heatwave of the summer in Spain.The fire in Ávila, which has burned more than 43,000 hectares over the past week, is now considered the largest recorded wildfire in Spanish history. A small amount of rain fell near Bordeaux in France on Thursday, raising hopes that the Gironde wildfire that has burned an area larger than the US city of Detroit and destroyed 240 homes might soon be over.The region's fire service said it was "reasonably optimistic" given that the fire had not grown in size since the weekend.Around 84,000 of the 220,000 displaced residents were allowed to return home on Thursday, according to French reports.It is estimated that more than 90,000 hectares of land across France have burnt this year - higher than any other year on record, according to data from the European Forest Fire Information Service.In Spain, more than 200,000 hectares have burnt in 2026 – roughly five times above the average for the time of year. The area of land ravaged in Portugal is also higher than usual for this point in July.The European fire season typically extends into August and September – and with more hot weather on the way in the coming days, these figures are likely to keep rising.Most wildfires are started by humans, whether deliberately or accidentally, but climate change is strengthening weather conditions conducive to fires spreading.Last winter was mild and wet, encouraging vegetation growth, which has then dried out in successive heatwaves, generating tinder-dry fuel for wildfires.Some researchers have also warned that the Mediterranean's forests and scrublands are not being properly managed – leaving plenty of vegetation as fuel for fires.Forecasters say fire-prone conditions are expected to spread towards central Europe, with Greece and Turkey among the countries worst affected.In Turkey, hundreds of homes have also been evacuated but the majority of fires that have broken out mainly in the south have been brought under control, authorities say.

schema.headline: Thousands evacuated in Crete as Europe battles wildfires

title: Eddie Howe: Does Newcastle manager's departure mark the beginning of the end of Saudi dream?
description: So what are the rules that Newcastle have, at times, come close to breaking?From the beginning of the PIF takeover, Profit and Sustainability Rules (P
body: So what are the rules that Newcastle have, at times, come close to breaking?From the beginning of the PIF takeover, Profit and Sustainability Rules (PSR) have put the brakes on Newcastle's ambitions to spend.Just because a club has wealthy owners does not mean they can spend big in the transfer windows.After buying the club in 2021, PIF spent £404.7m in the first three years. But by bringing in only £50.4m from sales, Newcastle saw the stark reality of PSR hit home in 2024.That led to them having to sell homegrown talent Elliot Anderson to Nottingham Forest and has snowballed since, with important players being offloaded every season.The Magpies welcomed the new Financial Fair Play rules - the Squad Cost Ratio (SCR), which are now in effect - and, in short, mean the more you generate, the more you can spend.But, when analysing their spending power against that of other Premier League clubs, Swiss Ramble, external found that the Magpies' SCR budget ranked ninth (£243m) in the Premier League.On top of that, in April the PIF withdrew its multibillion dollar backing of LIV Golf after Yasir Al-Rumayyan - the fund's governor and chairman of Newcastle - confirmed the PIF was reviewing its deals and investments.In turn, questions were raised about what that meant for the future of Newcastle - but senior club figures were informed at the time that the pullout did not affect the club. The fund is still viewed as being engaged.In the club's most recent set of accounts from last season, Newcastle's revenues have more than doubled to £335.3m - from the £140.2m recorded in the final full campaign of Mike Ashley's ownership.There are also plans for a new state-of-the-art training ground while Hopkinson has outlined a desire to revamp St James' Park or move stadiums to increase matchday revenue.The potential appointment of former RB Salzburg boss Jaissle is also intriguing given he is currently in charge of Saudi Arabian side Al-Ahli - a club the PIF held a majority stake in until selling it in April.

schema.headline: Eddie Howe: Does Newcastle manager's departure mark the beginning of the end of Saudi dream?

title: UK warned about 'explosive diarrhoea' cyclospora infection
description: UK holidaymakers are being warned about a nasty infectious disease called cyclosporiasis that can cause explosive diarrhoea, after a sharp rise in cas
body: UK holidaymakers are being warned about a nasty infectious disease called cyclosporiasis that can cause explosive diarrhoea, after a sharp rise in cases.The UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA), external said 67 cases have been reported since April, with many of them among travellers returning from Mexico.It comes amid an outbreak in the US that has infected more than 18,000 people across 45 states. The source hasn't been identified yet and there have been no reported deaths.The illness is caused by a parasite, cyclospora, that can contaminate food like salads, herbs and soft fruits. It doesn't naturally occur in the UK and there is no risk of spread from person to person, experts stress.Between 30 April and 15 July 2026, 30 cases have been reported in England, 27 in Scotland and 10 in Wales, according to the UKHSA.Of the 52 cases with travel information available, 48 reported having travelled to Mexico, with many saying they had stayed in either the white sand beach resort area of Riviera Maya, or slightly north of there in coastal Cancún.The UKHSA said those affected reported staying in "a range of different hotels and consuming a variety of different food and drink within their resort as part of an all-inclusive holiday package".There are ongoing investigations and monitoring of the situation. People can protect themselves while away by following good food and water hygiene measures, including drinking bottled water and eating thoroughly cooked food, even when staying in high-end all-inclusive resorts. Experts also advise people avoid certain foods such as fresh uncooked berries and herbs, unpeeled fruit and salad items.Some who have been struck by it describe having to use the toilet up to 20 times a day, due to the frequent and explosive nature of the watery diarrhoea that's the main symptom.The intestinal illness has recently affected thousands of people in the US. Nick Palmiter, who is 29 and from Monroe County in Michigan, told the BBC he experienced feeling constant pressure and bubbling, "almost like you have a balloon in your stomach".Although most cases resolve on their own, antibiotics can be given to treat severe or prolonged infections.The UKHSA said it anticipates there will be more cases linked to increased summer travel to Mexico and possibly the US too.Dr Philip Veal from the agency said: "If you develop symptoms after returning from travel, such as watery diarrhoea, loss of appetite, weight loss, stomach cramps or pain, bloating, increased wind, nausea, fatigue or other flu-like symptoms, please seek medical attention and inform your healthcare professional of your travel history."

schema.headline: UK warned about 'explosive diarrhoea' cyclospora infection
